questions.question: What is Verilog and why is it called a Hardware Description Language? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Verilog is a Hardware Description Language (HDL) used to design, model, simulate, and
  • verify digital electronic circuits and systems. It is called a Hardware Description Language
  • because:
  • It describes the structure and behaviour of digital circuits.
  • It represents hardware components such as logic gates, multiplexers, counters, and flip-flops.
  • It allows designers to simulate and test circuit operation before implementing the hardware.
  • It is used to design and implement digital circuits on devices such as FPGA and ASIC.
  • [K] / [CO1]
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the operation of a 3-to-8 decoder. Derive the Boolean expression for each output. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• A 3-to-8 decoder is a combinational logic circuit that has 3 input lines and 8 output lines.
  • For each input combination, only one output is HIGH (1), while all the other outputs remain
  • LOW (0). A 3-to-8 decoder converts a 3-bit binary input into one of 8 active outputs using the
  • corresponding Boolean expressions. Let the inputs be 𝐴, 𝐵, 𝐶and the outputs be 𝑌0to 𝑌7.
  • The 3 inputs can represent 23 = 8 different combinations.
  • Each input combination activates one unique output.
  • The decoder is used in memory address decoding and digital systems.
  • Verilog Code (Dataflow Modeling)
  • verilog
  • module decoder3to8 (
  • input A, B, C,
  • output [7:0] Y
  • );
  • assign Y[0] = ~A & ~B & ~C;
  • assign Y[1] = ~A & ~B & C;
  • assign Y[2] = ~A & B & ~C;
  • assign Y[3] = ~A & B & C;
  • assign Y[4] = A & ~B & ~C;
  • assign Y[5] = A & ~B & C;
  • assign Y[6] = A & B & ~C;
  • assign Y[7] = A & B & C;
  • endmodule [U] / [CO2]

questions.question: Explain the main components of a Verilog testbench. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• A Verilog testbench is used to simulate and verify the correct operation of a digital circuit
  • before hardware implementation. The main components of a Verilog testbench are:
  • Module Declaration: Defines the testbench module. It usually has no input or output ports.
  • Instantiation of DUT: The Design Under Test (DUT) is the circuit being tested and is
  • instantiated inside the testbench.
  • Stimulus Generation: Provides input signals to the DUT to test its functionality.
  • Monitoring and Verification: Observes the output signals and checks whether the outputs match
  • the expected results. [K] / [CO3]

questions.question: What is meant by concurrency in Verilog? How is it different from sequential execution in a conventional programming language? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Concurrency means that multiple hardware operations execute simultaneously. In Verilog,
  • independent always blocks and continuous assign statements operate concurrently. Verilog
  • supports concurrency to model the parallel behaviour of digital hardware, whereas
  • conventional programming languages generally follow sequential execution.
  • Difference between Concurrency and Sequential Execution:
  • Concurrency in Verilog Sequential Execution
  • Multiple operations occur simultaneously. Statements execute one after another.
  • Represents the parallel operation of hardware
  • circuits.
  • Commonly used in conventional programming
  • languages like C.
  • Independent always blocks execute
  • concurrently.
  • Statements generally execute in the order
  • written.
  • Example: Two registers can be updated at the
  • same clock edge.
  • One statement executes after the previous
  • statement completes.
  • [U] / [CO1]

  • Boolean expression:

  • XNOR Gate (Exclusive-NOR): The output of an XNOR gate is HIGH (1) when the two inputs

questions.question: Explain the operation of a 4-bit shift register. Discuss serial-in serial-out (SISO) with suitable Verilog statements. / [CO3] [5x4 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• A 4-bit shift register is a sequential circuit consisting of four flip-flops connected in series.
  • It stores 4 bits of data and shifts the data by one position for every clock pulse. At every positive
  • edge of the clock, the input bit sin enters the register, and the existing bits shift one position
  • towards the output. The most significant bit q[3] is available at the serial output sout.
  • Serial-In Serial-Out (SISO): Data is entered one bit at a time through the serial input. At every
  • active clock edge, the data shifts by one position. The data is obtained one bit at a time from
  • the serial output. A 4-bit SISO register requires four clock pulses to load four bits of data.
  • Verilog Code:
  • verilog
  • module SISO (
  • input clk, sin,
  • output sout
  • );
  • reg [3:0] q;
  • always @(posedge clk)
  • q <= {q[2:0], sin};
  • assign sout = q[3];
  • endmodule [U] / [CO3]

questions.question: Explain the operation of a Full Subtractor. Design and implement a Full Subtractor using gate-level modeling with wire elements. Write a suitable testbench to verify its operation. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• A Full Subtractor is a combinational logic circuit that subtracts two bits 𝐵and 𝐵𝑖𝑛from input
  • bit 𝐴. The full subtractor performs subtraction of three input bits and produces the difference
  • and borrow outputs. The gate -level Verilog design uses logic primitives and wire elements,
  • while the testbench verifies all eight input combinations. It has three inputs and two outputs.
  • Inputs: 𝐴(minuend), 𝐵(subtrahend), 𝐵𝑖𝑛(borrow input).
  • Outputs: 𝐷(difference), 𝐵𝑜𝑢𝑡(borrow output).
  • The Boolean expression for the difference is:
  • 𝐷 = 𝐴 ⊕ 𝐵 ⊕ 𝐵𝑖𝑛
  • The Boolean expression for the borrow output is:
  • 𝐵𝑜𝑢𝑡 = 𝐴‾ 𝐵 + 𝐴‾ 𝐵𝑖𝑛 + 𝐵𝐵𝑖𝑛
  • Verilog Code Using Gate-Level Modelling - Gate-level modelling uses logic gate primitives
  • such as xor, and, or, and not. The intermediate signals are declared using wire.
  • verilog
  • module full_subtractor(
  • input A, B, Bin,
  • output D, Bout
  • );
  • wire x1, nA, w1, w2, w3;
  • xor (x1, A, B);
  • xor (D, x1, Bin);
  • not (nA, A);
  • and (w1, nA, B);
  • and (w2, nA, Bin);
  • and (w3, B, Bin);
  • or (Bout, w1, w2, w3);
  • endmodule
  • A testbench applies all eight possible input combinations and displays the outputs.
  • [A] / [CO2]

questions.question: Explain the basic structure of a Verilog program. Describe the purpose of modules, ports, declarations, and statements / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Verilog is a Hardware Description Language (HDL) used to design, simulate, and verify
  • digital electronic circuits. The basic structure of a Verilog program consists of modules, ports,
  • declarations, and statements. These components help describe, simulate, and verify digital
  • circuits efficiently.
  • The general structure of a Verilog program is:
  • verilog
  • module module_name (ports);
  • // Port declarations
  • // Signal declarations
  • // Continuous assignments
  • // Procedural statements
  • endmodule
  • A Verilog program consists of one or more modules. Each module describes a particular digital
  • circuit or hardware component.
  • Main Components
  • Modules
  • • A module is the basic building block of a Verilog program.
  • • It defines a digital circuit or hardware component.
  • • A module begins with module and ends with endmodule.
  • Example:
  • verilog
  • module AND_GATE (A, B, Y);
  • Ports
  • • Ports are used to communicate signals between a module and its external environment.
  • • The three main port types are:
  • o input – receives signals.
  • o output – sends signals.
  • o inout – supports bidirectional signals.
  • Example:
  • verilog
  • input A, B;
  • output Y;
  • Declarations
  • Declarations define the type and size of signals used in a module. Common declarations
  • include:
  • wire – represents connections between hardware components.
  • reg – stores a procedural variable value and can represent combinational or sequential logic.
  • integer – represents an integer variable, often used in testbenches.
  • Example:
  • verilog
  • wire temp;
  • reg Q;
  • Statements
  • Statements describe the operation of the circuit.
  • assign – performs continuous assignment.
  • always – describes procedural behaviour.
  • initial – executes a procedural block once at the start of simulation. [U] / [CO1]

questions.question: From the following Verilog declarations and answer the questions that follow: wire [7:0] data; reg [3:0] count; integer i; real voltage; time delay; (a) Identify the data type of each declaration. (b) State the number of bits specified for data and count. (c) Mention the purpose of integer, real, and time. (d) Explain why different data types are required in Verilog HDL. (e) Write suitable Verilog declarations for a 16-bit signal and an 8-bit procedural variable. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• (a) Data types
  • data: Net (wire)
  • count: Register (reg)
  • i: Integer (integer)
  • voltage: Real (real)
  • delay: Time (time)
  • (b) Number of bits
  • data: 8 bits
  • count: 4 bits
  • (c) integer: Loop counters and arithmetic calculations
  • real: Storing floating-point/decimal numbers in simulation
  • time: Storing simulation time
  • (d) To differentiate physical wiring (wire) from storage elements (reg)
  • To separate hardware design constructs from simulation/testbench variables
  • To support both continuous assignments and procedural assignments
  • (e) Declarations - 16-bit signal: wire [15:0] signal;

questions.question: Explain the design and behavioral modeling of a 2-to-4 decoder. Include its block diagram description, truth table, Verilog code and applications. / [CO3] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• A decoder is a combinational circuit that converts binary information from n input lines
  • into a maximum of 2ⁿ unique output lines. A 2×4 decoder takes 2 input bits and activates one
  • of four output lines depending on the input combination. It’s widely used in memory address
  • decoding, data routing, and control circuits.
  • Behavioral modeling describes the operation of a circuit using procedural statements such as
  • always and case.
  • verilog
  • module decoder2to4(
  • input [1:0] A,
  • output reg [3:0] Y
  • );
  • always @(*) begin
  • case (A)
  • 2'b00: Y = 4'b0001;
  • 2'b01: Y = 4'b0010;
  • 2'b10: Y = 4'b0100;
  • 2'b11: Y = 4'b1000;
  • default: Y = 4'b0000;
  • endcase
  • end
  • endmodule
  • Applications - Memory address decoding / Instruction decoding / Display systems / Data
  • routing. [U] / [CO3]
